claim: Human-AI teams on average do worse than the better of human or AI alone (Hedges g -0.23, 106 experiments, 370 effect sizes), but better than humans alone (g 0.64).
agent_test: Compare scaffold arm to plain model arm at equal tokens; require scaffold > best single arm, not just > weak arm. One meta-analysis plus Bansal Table 1 examples.
audit_note: Vaccaro et al. also report very high heterogeneity (I2 about 97.7%) and that the negative synergy was driven by decision tasks; Bansal et al. is a separate paper on explanations.

claim: Decision tasks lose and content-creation tasks gain from pairing (g -0.27 vs +0.19 n.s.); the creation gain is not significant alone.
agent_test: Split bench items into decide-from-options vs generate; test whether extra checking steps help only the generative class.

claim: Pairing helps when the human side is better alone (g +0.46) and hurts when the AI side is better alone (g -0.54); over 95% of systems gave the human the final say.
agent_test: Where the model beats the program check on an item class, let the model answer stand; test a program veto only where the checker is stronger.

claim: Explanations do not reliably improve team accuracy over a confidence display; they raise acceptance of the AI answer right or wrong.
agent_test: Add rationale text to the verifier input vs confidence only; measure acceptance of wrong candidates.
audit_note: Bansal et al. abstract states explanations did not increase complementary performance and raised acceptance regardless of correctness; Vaccaro et al. find explanation and confidence moderators not significant. Scope is AI with accuracy comparable to humans, three tasks.

claim: Overreliance is a cost-benefit choice: explanations cut it only when checking is cheaper than redoing the task; hard-to-read explanations raise it.
agent_test: Make the check cheap and structured (diff, test result) rather than prose; compare verifier accuracy on wrong candidates.

claim: Forcing the person to commit before seeing the AI answer reduces overreliance but does not remove it, and the team stays below the AI alone.
agent_test: Have the verifier produce its own answer before seeing the candidate; compare acceptance of wrong candidates at equal tokens.

claim: Hedged first-person uncertainty in LLM output lowers user agreement and raises accuracy in medical QA; unhedged AI access lowered accuracy versus no AI (63.9% vs 74.2%).
agent_test: Attach a calibrated confidence to candidates passed to a checker and measure checker error on wrong candidates.
audit_note: Numbers match (63.9% vs 74.2%; 88.5/77.9; 33.0/64.7). Caveat: the AI was a fictional LLM search engine with built-in errors, so 'unhedged AI lowered accuracy' is specific to that design; also general-perspective hedging was weaker (67.9%, not significant) and Steyvers is not about hedging.

claim: Longer LLM explanations raise human confidence without raising accuracy; users overestimate LLM accuracy; convincing wrong explanations mislead (accuracy 0.35 when explanation wrong).
agent_test: Compare checker accuracy given short vs long candidate rationale; give the checker a for-argument and an against-argument.
audit_note: Steyvers et al. show length bias in confidence without accuracy gain (284 analysed of 301; 0.46 vs 0.95 example item); Si et al. report 0.35 (+/-0.22) accuracy when the ChatGPT explanation is wrong vs 0.56 with contrastive explanation (p=0.009).

claim: Measured and felt productivity can differ in sign: experienced developers were 19% slower with AI while believing 20% faster.
agent_test: Always log measured outcome at equal tokens; never accept self-judged improvement as the score.

claim: Two randomised trials point in opposite directions: GitHub Copilot cut completion time 55.8% on a self-contained HTTP-server task (95 developers, Peng et al. 2023), while allowing AI made 16 experienced developers 19% slower on 246 real issues in mature repos (METR 2025); the studies differ in tool, year, task and population, so the cause of the difference is not established.
agent_test: State the task class for every scaffold claim; test on both short-specified and long-context items.
audit_note: Numbers match (95 developers, 55.8% less time, p=0.0017; 16 developers, 246 tasks, 19% more time), but the trials also differ in year, tool, population and task, and neither paper tests that task or expertise explains the sign difference (Peng only reports larger gains for less experienced developers).
claim_before_audit: Randomised trials give opposite signs for coding assistants depending on task and expertise: 55.8% faster (greenfield, N=95) vs 19% slower (mature repos, 16 devs, 246 tasks).

claim: The weaker partner gains most from AI assistance: +34% for novices vs minimal for experts (5,179 agents); bottom-half skill gained more in the consultant study.
agent_test: Test scaffold gain on a small vs large model at equal tokens; expect larger gain on the smaller.
audit_note: Brynjolfsson et al.: 5,179 agents, +14% average, +34% for novice/low-skilled, minimal for experienced (lowest skill quintile +34%); Dell'Acqua et al. (Organization Science 2026 version, via a mirror) report bottom-half-skill subjects as the main beneficiaries. Different tasks (customer support vs consulting).

claim: AI helps inside the capability frontier and hurts outside it (consultants: +12.2% tasks, 25.1% faster inside; about 19 points less correct on the one outside task).
agent_test: Measure scaffold gain by item difficulty tier; check it does not hurt the hardest tier.

claim: Multi-agent coordination gains depend on task decomposability: +80.8% on decomposable finance vs -70.0% on sequential planning; coordination is negative once a single agent exceeds about 45%.
agent_test: At equal tokens compare one model with a program loop vs extra model roles on sequential vs parallel items.

claim: A central verifier contains error spread: trace-level amplification 1.0 single, 4.4 centralized, 5.1 hybrid, 7.8 decentralized, 17.2 independent; but the amplification term was not significant after controls (p 0.658).
agent_test: Run centralized program check vs none; measure error propagation across steps.

claim: Multi-agent LLM failures split into system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9% and verification 21.3% (1642 traces, 7 frameworks); role clarity gave +9.4% and a verification step +15.6% on ChatDev.
agent_test: Add a program-side objective check to a failing pipeline; measure success change at equal tokens.

claim: Collaborative agents beat autonomous ones on win rate with real users (86/74/66%), but fail on communication (65%) and situational awareness (40%).
agent_test: Not testable on a single-agent benchmark; design warning that the model does not track shared state.

claim: LLMs presume common ground: GPT-3.5 produced 84.8% fewer clarification acts and 83.4% fewer acknowledgments than humans in tested sets; preference tuning worsened it.
agent_test: Test an explicit assumption-listing step on ambiguous items; measure accuracy and cost.

claim: Verification is a hidden cost in AI-assisted work: after accepting a suggestion unchecked, programmers verified afterward 53.2% of the time; evaluating replaces producing.
agent_test: Count checking tokens as part of the budget when comparing scaffold with plain.
audit_note: Minor: Mozannar's 53.2% is for suggestions accepted after 'deferred thought' (21 programmers, post-hoc verification raises mean verification time to 15.21 s from 3.25 s); Simkute et al. is a review without new data.

claim: Roles split: a program owns the decision loop and memory, the model is a callable component (CoALA); automation level and human control are separate axes.
agent_test: Descriptive, not a performance claim; no test.
audit_note: CoALA (modular memory, action space, decision procedure with the LLM as one component) and Shneiderman's two independent axes (automation and human control) both match; two separate sub-claims, each backed by one conceptual paper.

claim: Operator skill decays and take-over needs more skill when the process is abnormal; the irony carries over to generative AI.
agent_test: After a failed check, pass full failing output plus state summary vs bare retry; measure repair rate.
audit_note: Bainbridge (1983) states manual skills deteriorate when not practised and that take-over in abnormal conditions needs a more, not less, skilled operator; the generative-AI carry-over is Simkute et al.'s argument (review, no new data).

claim: Overreliance and forcing-function evidence comes from simulated or classifier AI and crowd tasks; direct evidence on LLM checkers of LLM candidates is missing.
agent_test: Run candidate-plus-checker with a same-family LLM checker and a different-family one.

claim: The functional definition of a joint cognitive system and COCOM control modes (scrambled, opportunistic, tactical, strategic) come from Hollnagel and Woods; the mode table was read second-hand from Hollnagel 1993; the Stanton 2001 test was seen only as an abstract.
agent_test: No test until the primary text is read; framing only.

claim: An LLM used as its own checker mostly fails by rejecting correct answers (GPT-4 accepted 30 of 500 colorings, 5 right) and gives no net gain; a sound program verifier gives 34-38% on Game of 24 and coloring against 16% or less standard.
agent_test: Same task, program verifier vs model verifier at equal samples.
audit_note: Minor: the two Stechly papers share a lab (Kambhampati group), so the specific numbers (30 of 500 accepted, 5 right; Game of 24 5% to 36-38%; coloring 16% to 34-38%) are one-lab evidence; Huang et al. and Kamoi et al. independently support the no-net-gain-from-self-critique point.

claim: LLM judges favour text that is their own or familiar (GPT-4 self-recognition 73.5%; bias tracks perplexity), so a same-family checker is not independent.
agent_test: Compare same-family vs other-family checker false-accept rate.
audit_note: Minor: 73.5% is out-of-the-box self-recognition of GPT-4 (Panickssery et al.); Wataoka et al. tie bias to low perplexity, not authorship. Neither paper tests a same-family (rather than same-model) checker, so that last step is an inference.

claim: Mixing model families improves multi-agent debate (+6.4% and +8.2% over single-model averages), while same-model debate rarely beats CoT or self-consistency.
agent_test: Equal-token test of a different-family checker; baseline must be best single model.

claim: Repeated sampling plus an exact program verifier turns coverage into accuracy; model-side selection plateaus near 100 samples (MATH 40.50 to 41.41% vs coverage 82.9 to 98.44%).
agent_test: Program verifier vs majority vote at equal samples.
audit_note: Minor: the 40.50 to 41.41% figure is the largest gain of majority vote or reward model across 100 to 10,000 samples (Llama-3-8B-Instruct on MATH), and coverage there is measured against ground truth (a perfect verifier); Stechly et al. add k=25 resampling with a sound verifier giving 42-44%.

claim: More calls help easy items and hurt hard items in vote systems; the best call count can be predicted from a small sample.
agent_test: Split bench by difficulty tier and test scaffold gain per tier.

claim: In multi-turn underspecified work LLMs drop 39% on average (aptitude -15%, unreliability +112%), over-relying on early assumptions and prior attempts; recap helps partly.
agent_test: Hand back a clean state summary vs full history after a failed check.

claim: COCOM control modes differ by goals, subjectively available time, action choice and evaluation; the only independent human test found (Stanton 2001) was seen as an abstract, and no LLM budget test was found.
agent_test: Map token budget to mode; test whether mode-matched prompts beat one fixed prompt.

claim: Still unanswered: no replication of the 45% saturation threshold, no token-cost comparison of verify vs plain, no felt-vs-measured study for LLM self-judging.
agent_test: Measure in our own harness.
